story.title: Protesters Break Into Microsoft Data Centre Construction Site in Amsterdam
story.summary: On November 6, over 100 activists stormed a construction site for a Microsoft data centre in Amsterdam. The protesters climbed cranes and displayed banners criticizing artificial intelligence and the company's alleged role in the conflict in Gaza.

explore_lenses.label: What changed on the ground after the breach?
explore_lenses.title: Police moved from containment to removals
explore_lenses.summary: The protest shifted from a planned public demonstration into an occupation of a private construction site, prompting enforcement action. The final number detained and the status of any criminal cases were not publicly settled in the reporting reviewed.

claims.text: Dutch public broadcaster NOS reported that demonstrators breached the perimeter at Plimsollweg in Sloterdijk and that police had deployed in large numbers before the planned Fossielvrij NL protest began.
The Associated Press reported that Dutch police said on Friday evening they had detained 150 to 200 people on suspicion of trespassing.

Under Dutch police guidance, a protest on public roads is governed differently from an occupation of private premises, which can fall under criminal trespass law; the decision to end such an action rests with the mayor and/or public prosecutor, not police alone.

explore_lenses.label: Why is the data-centre project still proceeding?
explore_lenses.title: Earlier permits and a legal definition shape the dispute
explore_lenses.summary: The project’s advance reflects permits issued before later national hyperscale restrictions, plus a government conclusion that the site does not meet the rule’s floor-area threshold. Its environmental permissions were still being contested as of the government’s April 2026 response.

claims.text: An Amsterdam permit notice records that approval to build DC Westpoort at Plimsollweg 3, 13 and 23 was granted on November 6, 2020.

In an April 2026 parliamentary response, the Dutch government said the 2020 construction permit predated national hyperscale rules and that the project fell outside those rules because its built floor area was below 10 hectares, even though the cited total connection capacity was 99 MW across three towers.
The same response said North Holland granted three environmental permits on July 15, 2025 and that an appeal against those permits was pending.

Organisers argue that the development worsens pressure on electricity capacity and local planning; Fossielvrij NL’s event notice framed the action as part of a Europe-wide call to halt new data centres.

explore_lenses.label: What is behind the Gaza-related accusation?
explore_lenses.title: A documented Microsoft–Israeli military relationship fuels the protest
explore_lenses.summary: The Gaza message rests on more than a general allegation: Microsoft acknowledges providing services to Israel’s Ministry of Defense. However, Microsoft disputes that its technology has been used to harm people in Gaza and says it acted after an external review found evidence supporting elements of reporting on specific services.

claims.text: Microsoft states that it provides Israel’s Ministry of Defense with software, professional services, Azure cloud services and Azure AI services, including translation; it describes this as a standard commercial relationship governed by its terms of service.

Microsoft’s published follow-up says Covington found evidence supporting elements of reporting about the ministry’s use of Azure storage in the Netherlands and AI services; Microsoft said it then ceased and disabled specified subscriptions and services.

Microsoft has said its earlier reviews found no evidence that its Azure or AI technologies were used to target or harm people in Gaza, while acknowledging limits on its visibility into customers’ use of software on their own systems and into non-Microsoft government-cloud operations.

At the Amsterdam protest, pro-Palestinian demonstrators said Microsoft bore responsibility for Palestinian oppression and linked data-centre infrastructure to surveillance and violence; this is the protesters’ position, not an independently adjudicated finding.

story_report.summary: More than 100 activists entered a Microsoft data-centre construction site in Amsterdam on November 6, climbing cranes and displaying banners opposing artificial intelligence and the war in Gaza. Dutch public broadcaster NOS reported that demonstrators breached the perimeter at Plimsollweg in Sloterdijk, where police had deployed in large numbers ahead of a planned Fossielvrij NL protest. Police later detained between 150 and 200 people on suspicion of trespassing, according to the Associated Press.

sections.heading: Trespass Rules Shape Police Response
sections.body: Dutch police guidance distinguishes between a demonstration on public roads and an occupation of private premises. An occupation can fall under criminal trespass law, while the decision to end such an action rests with the mayor and/or public prosecutor rather than police alone. The reported detentions were on suspicion of trespassing.

sections.heading: Westpoort Project Has Existing Permits
sections.body: The planned facility is DC Westpoort, at Plimsollweg 3, 13 and 23. Amsterdam’s construction approval was granted on November 6, 2020; the Dutch government has said the permit predated national hyperscale-data-centre rules and that the project fell outside them because its built floor area was below 10 hectares. The government cited total connection capacity of 99 MW across three towers. North Holland issued three environmental permits in July 2025, which were under appeal.

sections.heading: Protesters Challenge Microsoft’s Gaza Role
sections.body: Organisers have argued that the development would add pressure to electricity capacity and local planning, framing the action as part of a Europe-wide call to stop new data centres. Pro-Palestinian protesters also said Microsoft was responsible for Palestinian oppression and connected data-centre infrastructure to surveillance and violence. Microsoft says it has a standard commercial relationship with Israel’s Ministry of Defense involving software, Azure cloud and AI services; its published follow-up says it disabled specified services after an external review supported elements of reporting about use of Azure storage in the Netherlands and AI services.

unresolved.text: The reviewed sources do not establish a final arrest count, charges, injuries, damage assessment or whether construction was delayed beyond November 6.
The reviewed material does not verify the project’s annual electricity use or the protesters’ comparison with all Amsterdam households.

The sources do not establish that the planned Amsterdam facility will host or process Israeli military data, and they do not resolve wider allegations about particular military uses of Microsoft technology.

related_stories.title: UN Reports Severe Shelter Shortages for Millions Fleeing Sudan Conflict
related_stories.summary: The United Nations has reported that approximately 15.4 million people displaced by the ongoing conflict in Sudan are in urgent need of emergency shelter and essential household items. However, humanitarian organizations are struggling to meet these needs due to significant funding shortages, with fewer than 1 million of those in need having received assistance.

related_stories.title: Three Charged in $129 Million AI Fraud Scheme Targeting Corporations
related_stories.summary: Three foreign nationals have been charged in an alleged scheme that utilized AI technology to impersonate CEOs and attorneys, resulting in the theft of over $129 million. The victims included various companies across multiple sectors, such as hospital systems, banks, and financial technology firms in the U.S. and abroad.

related_stories.title: Judge Blocks Construction of Trump's Proposed Arch Following Federal Approval
related_stories.summary: A judge has halted the construction of a 250-foot arch proposed by Trump, which had recently received federal approval to proceed. The project was expected to begin shortly, with plans for the arch to serve as a military complex housing drones and other military equipment.

related_stories.title: Sailor Killed in Gulf Tanker Attack Amid Rising Tensions
related_stories.summary: A sailor was killed during an attack on the Marshall Islands-flagged tanker Velos Sapphire in the Persian Gulf on November 5. The tanker was reportedly empty of cargo and en route to Bahrain when it was struck. Iran has claimed responsibility for the attack, which is part of a broader escalation of assaults on shipping in the region, including two other vessels that were reported to be on fire.
